---
title: "The Three Types of Quotes"
---

# The Three Types of Quotes

Proper quoting is the single most critical defensive skill in Bash. Bash supports three quoting mechanisms, each with distinct semantic rules:

## 1. Single Quotes (`'...'`)

Single quotes preserve the literal value of every character within the quotes. No expansions occur—no parameter substitution, no command substitution, no arithmetic expansion, and no escape sequences.

```bash
# Literal string preservation
name="Alice"
echo 'Hello, $name! Today is $(date).'
# Output: Hello, $name! Today is $(date).
```

*Note:* You cannot include a single quote inside single quotes, even with a backslash (`'` does not work). To include a literal single quote, close the quote, insert an escaped quote, and reopen: `'Don'''t touch this'`.

## 2. Double Quotes (`"..."`)

Double quotes suppress word splitting and globbing, but allow:
* Parameter expansion (`$VAR`, `${VAR}`)
* Command substitution (`$(command)`)
* Arithmetic expansion (`$(( ... ))`)
* Escaped dollar signs (`\$`), backticks (`\``), double quotes (`\"`), and backslashes (`\\`).

```bash
greeting="Hello"
user="Bob"
echo "$greeting, $user! PID is $$"
# Output: Hello, Bob! PID is 1234
```

## 3. ANSI-C Quoting (`$'...'`)

ANSI-C quoting expands C-style backslash escape sequences into literal binary characters before execution:

```bash
# Newlines, tabs, and hex characters
newline_string=$'Line 1\nLine 2\tIndented'
echo "$newline_string"

# Carriage return in terminal status lines
printf $'Downloading...\r'
```
